subject: dwarfRifleman
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: dwarf rifleman with braided beard and blunderbuss.
Style: Blizzard/Warcraft.
reasoning:
I'm planning a Warcraft-style dwarf rifleman model: stocky build with oversized pauldrons, a braided beard, a tricorn hat or helmet, a flared-muzzle blunderbuss with brass fittings, a bandolier and backpack, plus a small rocky base with a barrel and grass, scaling the figure to roughly 1.4 units tall.

I'm working out the full proportions and skeleton rig using the builder's joint/chain API, mapping hip, spine, shoulder, and leg joint heights to get the exaggerated big-head, broad-shoulder dwarf look while keeping the module reasonably sized and correct given I can't test it directly.

Simplifying the neck into a single joint instead of a chain, then adding a head joint parented to it with a forward-facing direction.

For orienting body parts, I want to use descriptive local words like "left," "right," "up," and "forward" relative to each joint instead of raw coordinates, since that avoids axis confusion. I'll treat symmetric offsets using a sign variable so the same formula mirrors correctly on both sides of the body.

Actually, I'll switch to plain model-space coordinates computed from constants instead of local offsets, which is simpler and more deterministic — defining a head center point and building the skull as a scaled sphere, with a wide dwarf-style shape, large nose, brow ridge, and decal eyes.

For the eyes, I'll use a decal placed on the skull surface near the face, since a plain part sphere approach feels less convincing. I'm sketching a small SVG with an almond-shaped white eye, a bright blue iris, and a dark pupil, matching a heavy-browed dwarf look.

Now I'm working out the beard as a swept tube running from the chin downward, defining a flattened radius profile that tapers as it goes.

I'm also planning braids on either side as chains of tilted small ellipsoids finishing in a gold ring with tassels, plus mustache curls as swept beziers with tapering radii.

Thinking through proportions: the beard should hang from chin to roughly chest/belt height, with braids running a bit lower and finished with gold clasps, consistent with a dwarven aesthetic. I'm also considering the overall pose — leaning toward a relaxed stance with arms slightly extended away from the body so the blunderbuss can rest naturally across the chest.

I'll set the gun's length and position from grip to muzzle so it sits naturally in the dwarf's hand, then figure out what to do with the left arm—maybe resting open at the side rather than holding anything.

Now I'm working out the arm chains using inverse kinematics, placing shoulder joints and computing upper arm and forearm lengths so the hand targets land within reach, with elbow bend hints pointing back and outward for a natural pose.

Setting tube radii along the chain and planning forearm bracers as metal cylinder parts attached to the elbow joint for armor detail.

Now I'm sketching a helper for creating segments as rods between two points with tapered radii, bound to joints for proper rigging. For hands I'm planning chunky fists with palm boxes and tapering finger capsules, mindful of the joint budget limit when building out multiple fingers per hand.

For the left hand I'm giving each finger its own small chain of two joints plus a thumb, parented to the wrist bone, with slight curl and forward-down pointing. The right hand gripping the gun just gets simplified fist boxes with bump-like finger shapes instead of full joint chains to save on budget.

For the legs I'm sketching short, thick hip-knee-ankle chains with forward-bent knees, matching hip-to-ankle distances roughly to the proportions, then building tapered boots out of a cuff shaft plus a capsule foot shape instead of more complex lathed geometry.

I'm also planning a flat dark sole box and metal toe cap, adding an optional toe joint parented to the ankle, and giving the legs varying thickness with brown cloth pants and metal knee pads before moving on to the torso loft shape.

For the torso I'm defining loft stations along the spine from hips to shoulders with increasing width and height, then deciding how to attach the bone chain—considering a simple hips-spine bone pair versus a longer chain to keep things safe and manageable.

Now I'm thinking through the color scheme for the tunic, leaning toward an Ironforge dwarf rifleman look with blue tabard over bronze/leather armor, paired with ruddy dwarf skin tones and a fiery red-orange beard.

For the headgear I'm debating between a steel kettle helmet, tricorn hat, or brimmed goggled cap, ultimately leaning toward a simple round steel helmet to keep the model's complexity manageable.

Now I'm positioning the pauldrons—large dome shoulder armor with studded rims, placing each one symmetrically on either shoulder.

I realize the ring items default to the nearest bone unless I pass one explicitly, and since the pauldron needs to track the shoulder joint, I should explicitly bind it with a bone parameter rather than relying on inference. Now I'm thinking about the gorget/collar piece around the neck.

For the belt, since the torso cross-section is elliptical rather than circular, a simple lathe-generated ring band won't fit naturally -- I'd need to scale it non-uniformly or build it as a closed sweep around an ellipse instead to match the waist shape properly.

But I realize the joint's rotation may mirror local axes relative to world, since the spine joint is likely rotated 180° about Y to align default roll—so scaling in mesh-local z might not correspond to world z the way I assumed, since local axes could be flipped under that rotation.

So instead of relying on mesh scale potentially fighting joint orientation, I'll build the belt using a lathe geometry with explicit scale applied through b.part, writing a helper function that generates ring-band meshes from 2D profile points.

For the torso's breastplate, I'm extruding a chest outline shape facing forward, working out the correct x/y axis orientation so the extrusion thickness points outward in +z as intended.

But the beard will cover the chest plate entirely, so I should shorten the beard or make it braided, hanging mass to around chest height but leaving the plate visible.

Repositioning the braids outward so they don't overlap the emblem, with the badge centered in the free space between them. Now I'm thinking about adding a blue tabard that hangs from the belt in front of the thighs, extruded with thin cloth thickness.

Let me add a gold trim border around the tabard using a slightly larger extrude behind it, plus a textured emblem plane layered on top. For the backpack, I'm planning a leather pack box with bedroll, pot, and powder keg attached, positioned behind the torso with a flap on top and straps securing it.

Now I'm working out a diagonal bandolier strap across the chest, sweeping a rod from the shoulder down to the opposite hip with cartridge cylinders placed along its path, making sure the z-offset sits just above the chest's curved surface so it doesn't clip into the body.

I'll hand-tune the bandolier strap points with varying z-depth to drape naturally over the chest rather than fighting with the plate geometry.

Now moving to the blunderbuss prop: I'm planning its construction along a central axis from butt to muzzle, building the stock, grip, and barrel as tapered boxes and rods oriented to that axis direction.

Working out barrel details now - a flared cone muzzle, dark bore disc at the tip, and brass ring bands wrapped around using torus shapes aligned to the gun's axis. For the lock mechanism I'm adding a box with hammer, pan, sideplate, and a trigger guard, computing perpendicular "up" and "side" vectors via cross products so everything orients correctly relative to the gun's forward direction.

Positioning the gun itself: I set a base and muzzle point giving a slight upward tilt, then compute where the grip sits along that axis so the right hand's wrist target lines up with the gun's handle, checking the resulting distance against the shoulder joint to confirm it's reachable.

For the fist gripping the stock, I'm sketching a palm as a scaled sphere at the hand position and planning finger capsules that curl around the grip's axis like a wraparound ring rather than sitting flat against it, since the stock runs along the gun's length.

Simpler approach: stack four small tori around the axis as knuckle rings plus a palm sphere, giving a cheap gloved-fist look. I'm also noting extra details to add later like a ramrod under the barrel, brass trim bands, and an engraved stock plate, then moving on to positioning the left hand.

For the base, I'm settling on a hexagonal stone plinth with mossy cobblestone texture, a powder keg with brass "Ironforge" lettering, an ammo crate, and a small lantern post at the back-left to add height without exceeding the overall scale limit. I'll also scatter a few spent cartridges for extra detail, plus accessories like a pouch and powder horn hanging from the figure's hips.

I'm now figuring out exact placement so props don't overlap the subject's footprint, computing coordinates for the barrel, crate, and keg relative to the dwarf's hands, backpack, and gun butt to keep everything visually balanced without clutter.

I'm also placing a lantern post off to the side, positioning it beside the figure's left hand while keeping clear of the gun muzzle's trajectory.

Adding a base rim texture, then planning the texture set: eye, anvil emblem, grass blades, keg rune label, tabard trim pattern, beard strand cards, and bracer rune, starting with SVG definitions for the eye and the gold anvil emblem on a circle.

The tabard works best as a flat textured plane with alpha cutouts handling the pointed hem, cloth pattern, gold border, and emblem all baked into one texture rather than modeled geometry.

For the remaining details, I'm planning a keg label (powder skull/"BOOM" graphic), simple glowing lens parts for goggles, painted wood grain for planks, and a small rune-etched plate decal on the gun stock using a thin textured plane. The hat badge can just reuse the emblem texture, and skin gets a mottled paint treatment for the face.

I'm defining a shading helper that blends a darker and lighter tone of a base color based on surface normal direction, creating a warm-top/cool-bottom lighting effect for skin tones.

I also need to check the color budget — paints don't count against the flat color limit, so I can rely on paint functions for most materials and save string colors for a few cases. For the tunic I'm considering a mottled cloth texture wrapped in the tone shader, and I'm checking whether a `resolve` helper is exported from the SDK so I can accept flexible color inputs into my paint functions.

For the tone shader itself, I'm defining it so it resolves the base color and blends in shadow and warm highlight tones based on vertical normal direction using smoothstep. For metal parts I'll reuse the prebuilt metal helper from the clockwork kit, and for wood I'll apply a grain texture through the tone wrapper. Writing imports and setup code...

Defining more colors...

Still defining material palettes...

Defining stone texture patches, then setting up a mossy top paint rule and lathe profile for the base's grass-covered surface.

I realize the base needs to sit on the floor while the character stands on top of it, so I need to raise all the character's coordinates by the base height rather than letting feet sink into the ground.

Shifting the root translates the whole hierarchy including hips, so I just need to confirm the harness measures positions post-transform, which it should since it's computed from world matrices after construction.

Actually, simpler: I'll introduce a constant offset Y0=0.08 baked into a helper function that shifts every y-coordinate when defining joint positions, so all coordinates like head center stay consistent without manually shifting each part.
